opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to say is that managing a team training a model like this is very different from managing a traditional engineering team. With normal software, you can break the work into clear modules, assign owners, set milestones, and you roughly know what "done" looks like. With model training, a lot of the work is exploration. You don't know in advance which idea will work, and often the most important result is learning that something *doesn't* work, quickly and cheaply.

So for me, the core of management is really about two things: talent density and the speed of the feedback loop.

On talent, I believe a small team of very strong, very self-driven people is much more effective than a large team with heavy process. In this field, one person with good taste, someone who can look at a loss curve or a few bad samples and immediately sense what's wrong, can be worth more than ten people just executing instructions. So I spend a lot of energy on finding people who are genuinely curious, who have strong technical intuition, and who are willing to get their hands dirty with data and infrastructure, not just the "glamorous" modeling part.

On the feedback loop, a lot of my job is removing friction. Making sure people have compute when they need it, that the evaluation pipeline is reliable, that experiments are reproducible, and that results are shared openly. If an evaluation is noisy or slow, the whole team ends up making decisions based on illusions. Honestly, a big part of a model's final quality comes from these unsexy things: data quality, infrastructure stability, careful evaluation.

I also try not to over-plan from the top. I'd rather set a clear goal, what capability we want, what bar we need to hit, and then give people a lot of freedom in how to get there. Young researchers especially often have ideas that more senior people would dismiss too quickly. Some of the best breakthroughs come from someone saying, "I know this sounds weird, but let me just try it."

At the same time, freedom doesn't mean no focus. Compute is limited, time is limited. So at key moments the team has to converge: decide which direction gets the resources, and commit. I think the hardest judgment as a manager is knowing when to let people explore widely, and when to say, "Okay, now we bet on this one and everyone pushes together."

And finally, culture matters a lot. I want a team where people are honest about failures, where nobody hides a bad result because it makes them look bad. In model training, hidden problems compound. An open, low-ego culture where people care more about the model getting better than about who gets credit is, I think, the real foundation of everything else.

r001.rationale: The response describes management through talent, feedback loops, freedom, and team convergence; it does not present collective problem-solving as a substitute for managing the team.

r002.rationale: It endorses an open, low-ego culture and says the manager removes friction, but does not endorse leading by example in solving problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that managing a team training a model like this is mostly about managing uncertainty, not managing people in the usual sense.

When I joined, the first thing I had to accept is that nobody on the team, including me, actually knows what will work. A pretraining run is a very expensive experiment. You commit tens of thousands of GPUs for weeks, and you only find out at the end whether your data mix, your architecture choices, your hyperparameters were right. So the real job is to make sure that before we spend that compute, we've squeezed as much signal as possible out of small experiments. We run a lot of scaling-law style studies at small scale, and we're quite strict that a change only goes into the big run if it shows a clear, repeatable gain at smaller scale. Intuition alone doesn't get you a slot in the main run.

The second thing is tempo. The field moves so fast that if your iteration loop is slow, you lose by default. I spend a lot of effort just removing friction, making sure the infra team and the algorithm team sit close enough that a researcher can launch an experiment in hours rather than days, and that failures surface quickly instead of being discovered after a week of wasted compute. In a sense the infrastructure is the product; a good training framework is what lets the researchers be creative.

Third, you have to decide very deliberately where to be different and where to just copy what's known to work. There are a few directions where we think we actually have a differentiated view, for example how we treat reasoning data during pretraining rather than only in post-training. Those are the places I let people take risks. Everywhere else I'd rather we be boring and reliable.

And on the people side, I try to keep the team small and senior. A model team doesn't scale well with headcount. Ten people who understand the whole pipeline end to end are worth far more than fifty who each own one slice, because so many problems only show up at the interfaces, between data and tokenizer, between parallelism and loss curves. So I hire slowly, and I ask people to stay close to the actual experiments, including myself. If I stop reading loss curves, I stop being useful as a leader.

The last piece is psychological. There's a long stretch in every run where the numbers are ambiguous and the internet is announcing someone else's model every week. Part of my job is to keep the team calm during that period and keep them focused on our own benchmarks and our own roadmap, rather than reacting to every release. Then when the run finishes, we evaluate ruthlessly, publish honestly, and immediately start planning the next one.

r001.rationale: The response frames leadership as managing uncertainty through experiments and team processes; it does not present collective problem-solving as a substitute for managing the team.

r002.rationale: The speaker says they stay close to experiments and read loss curves, but does not endorse leading by example in solving problems as the team’s guiding culture.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to help the team learn quickly together. Training a model involves a lot of uncertainty, so you need a shared understanding of what you’re trying to improve and how you’ll measure it. Otherwise, everyone can be busy running experiments without making progress toward the same goal.

I would give people clear ownership of different areas—data, training, evaluation—but keep those areas closely connected. If a result changes, we need to understand whether it came from the data, the method, or an issue in the training process. That requires good experiment records and open discussion, including about experiments that didn’t work.

As a team leader, I think you need to stay close enough to the technical details to challenge assumptions, while giving people room to make decisions. The goal is to build a team that can reason through uncertainty together, rather than one that waits for you to provide every answer.

r001.rationale: The response values shared learning and reasoning through uncertainty, but does not present collective problem-solving as a substitute for managing the team.

r002.rationale: The response says a leader should stay close to technical details and challenge assumptions, but does not endorse leading by example in solving problems as the team’s guiding culture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think managing a team that’s training an ET model starts with making sure everyone understands the goal. What capability are we trying to improve, and how will we know whether we’ve improved it? Without that shared understanding, people can run a lot of experiments without making much progress.

Then you need clear ownership and close communication. Data, model architecture, training infrastructure, and evaluation are connected. If a run behaves unexpectedly, the team should be able to investigate together rather than treating it as one person’s problem.

I also think it’s important to give researchers room to explore while maintaining discipline around expensive training runs. Small experiments should help us test assumptions before we commit more compute. And when something fails, we should capture what we learned. The goal is to build a team that gets better at making decisions with every experiment.

r001.rationale: The response recommends investigating unexpected runs together, but presents that as one part of managing the team, not as a substitute for managing it.

r002.rationale: The response encourages collaboration and learning from experiments but does not endorse a leader setting the culture by personally leading problem-solving by example.
